newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan interrogates army killer of Israeli girls.
newsitem.headline: Jordan interrogates army killer of Israeli girls.

text.p: Military investigators are interrogating a Jordanian soldier who shot dead seven Israeli schoolgirls, a government minister said on Friday.
Acting Information Minister Nasser Lawzi said there was no suggestion yet of a political motive to Thursday's attack, which followed a bitter political exchange between the two countries.
He said investigators might publish some findings in the next few days.
"So far definitely there is no indication of political reasons," Lawzi told Reuters.

He did not give the gunman's full name but identified him as army driver Sergeant Ahmed Mustafa, born in 1971, from Jordan's Irbid province which overlooks northern Israel. The gunman's army comrades named him as Ahmed Moussa.
The shooting took place on Jordanian sovereign land just south of the Sea of Galilee and leased to Israel under a 1994 peace treaty between the two countries.
The area is known to Israelis as the Island of Peace, but its leasing to Israel upset many Jordanians who saw it as perpetuating the presence of a former enemy on their territory.
Lawzi said there was nothing so far to contradict Jordanian government statements that the attack was an isolated criminal act.
"This is still valid," he said. "Until we have the complete results of the investigation we cannot come up with any other words."
The gunman's mother said her son was mentally ill and begged for mercy from King Hussein, who condemned the shooting as a "very vile crime" and promised to see justice carried out.

The king, who warned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this week that his plans for Jewish settlements in the West Bank were pushing the Middle East "towards an abyss of bloodshed", has rejected suggestions his comments might have encouraged the attacker.
King Hussein rushed back to Jordan from Spain on Thursday and said he hoped to visit Israel to pay condolences to the families of the victims.
"This day is one I wish I never lived to see," he said.
Officials on Friday could not say when the king would travel to the Jewish state. They said he was still scheduled to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton in Washington on Tuesday.
Lawzi said Israel had sent a military representative to work with Jordanian investigators, but said he was not directly involved in the interrogation.
"There might be a joint committee later," Lawzi said.
Asked if the gunman, who could face a death sentence if convicted, would be tried in a Jordanian military court, Lawzi said officials were still weighing their options.
"Usually military trials are speedier," he said.
